PRESCRIPTIVE EASEMENT AND EASEMENT BY NECESSITY — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Taylor Morgan

DECLARATION OF THE USE HISTORY SUPPORTING A CLAIMED PRESCRIPTIVE EASEMENT OR EASEMENT BY NECESSITY
Jordan Alex Lee ("Claimant") states the following regarding a claimed right to use real property located at 125 Main St, Sacramento, CA 95814, described as Lot 6, Block 2, per map recorded in Book 8, Page 12 (the "Servient Property"), also identified by Assessor's Parcel Number 456-789-012, provided for identification only and not as part of the Servient Property's legal description, situated in Sacramento County County, California, claimed for the benefit of real property owned by Claimant located at 123 Main St, Sacramento, CA 95814, described as Lot 5, Block 2, per map recorded in Book 8, Page 12 ("Claimant's Property").

The record owner of the Servient Property, as reflected in the county records known to Claimant, is Taylor Morgan.

If this claim rests on prescriptive use, Claimant's use of the Servient Property is described as having begun on January 1, 2018, and consists of the following: a gravel driveway used openly to access the rear parcel. This description states the manner, frequency, and visibility of Claimant's use. It does not state that Claimant's use has excluded the record owner, or any other person, from also using the same area, and it does not state that Claimant has paid property taxes assessed against the Servient Property; a claimed easement, unlike a claim of full ownership by adverse possession, does not require either.

If this claim rests instead, or in addition, on Claimant's Property having become landlocked as a result of a division of land once commonly owned, Claimant states that Riley Chen owned both Claimant's Property and the Servient Property as a single, undivided parcel until January 1, 2015, the date of the conveyance that separated them, and that Claimant's Property has had no legally adequate access to a public road since that severance.

This declaration is Claimant's own factual account of use, ownership, and severance history with respect to the Servient Property and Claimant's Property. It states facts as recounted by Claimant; it does not itself determine whether those facts satisfy the elements of a prescriptive easement or an easement by necessity under California law, and it does not itself create, convey, record, or adjudicate any easement. A determination that an easement exists, if sought, is made by a court, not by this document.

THE ELEMENTS OF A PRESCRIPTIVE EASEMENT AND ITS BORROWED FIVE-YEAR PERIOD
California has no statute that separately names and defines a "prescriptive easement" the way Code of Civil Procedure §§ 322 and 324 name and define adverse possession under color of title or under a bare claim of right (addressed in this corpus's separate Adverse Possession — Information Sheet document). Instead, California's courts have developed the doctrine as case law. California's Supreme Court has stated its elements directly: "The elements necessary to establish a prescriptive easement are well settled. The party claiming such an easement must show use of the property which has been open, notorious, continuous and adverse for an uninterrupted period of five years." Five years is also the period Code of Civil Procedure § 321 states for adverse possession generally, within the same statutory chapter governing the time for commencing an action to recover real property. A prescriptive easement claimed over the Servient Property at 125 Main St, Sacramento, CA 95814 for the benefit of Claimant's Property at 123 Main St, Sacramento, CA 95814 differs from adverse possession in what it can produce even when proven: adverse possession, if established, can transfer fee title to the possessor; a prescriptive easement, even if established, transfers only a right to use another's land for a stated purpose — the kind of right this corpus's Easement Agreement document addresses when it is created by grant rather than by this doctrine. Establishing a prescriptive easement does not make Claimant the owner of the Servient Property.

NO EXCLUSIVITY AND NO TAX-PAYMENT REQUIREMENT: HOW A PRESCRIPTIVE EASEMENT DIFFERS FROM ADVERSE POSSESSION
California case law directly distinguishes a prescriptive easement from adverse possession on two points commonly, and correctly, described as required for adverse possession but not for a prescriptive easement: exclusivity of use, and payment of property taxes. A California Court of Appeal has explained the two doctrines side by side: "Adverse possession is a means to acquire ownership of land. In adverse possession, the claimant must prove open and notorious use, hostile to the true owner, for a period of five years, and he must also show that he has paid taxes on the parcel of land. By comparison, an easement is merely a right to use the land of another." California's adverse possession statute independently confirms the tax-payment half of that comparison — it requires a claimant to have "timely paid all state, county, or municipal taxes" levied on the land for the full statutory period before adverse possession is established under any section of the Code of Civil Procedure, a requirement addressed in this corpus's Adverse Possession — Information Sheet document. The case law above states a narrow exception on the easement side of that same comparison: "if taxes are separately assessed against an easement, the claimant must pay these" — a circumstance the same court described as unusual. On exclusivity, the same court held it was error to award a claimant an easement that, as a practical matter, completely excluded the record owner from the area, reasoning that "[a]n easement, after all, is merely the right to use the land of another for a specific purpose" and "is not an ownership interest," so that treating a claimant's use as exclusive "perverts the classical distinction in real property law between ownership and use." This document's use-history declaration accordingly describes Claimant's use of the Servient Property at 125 Main St, Sacramento, CA 95814 as a use, not as an exclusion of Taylor Morgan or any other person from the same area, and does not state that Claimant has paid property taxes assessed against the Servient Property unless the easement area has been separately assessed for tax purposes.

EASEMENT BY NECESSITY: COMMON OWNERSHIP AT SEVERANCE AND STRICT NECESSITY
California has no Civil Code provision that separately creates or names an "easement by necessity" the way Civil Code § 1104 creates a different implied easement out of a transferred property's own prior, obvious, and permanent use (addressed in this corpus's Easement Agreement document). The necessity doctrine is instead stated by California's courts as case law, with two elements: "An easement by way of necessity arises by operation of law when it is established that (1) there is a strict necessity for the right-of-way, as when the claimant's property is landlocked and (2) the dominant and servient tenements were under the same ownership at the time of the conveyance giving rise to the necessity." California case law also states what "strict necessity" requires, as distinct from mere convenience: "The right of way from necessity must be in fact what the term naturally imports and cannot exist except in cases of strict necessity. It will not exist when a man can get to his property over his own land. That the way over his own land is too steep or too narrow or that other and like difficulties exist, does not alter the case, and it is only when there is no way through his own land that a grantee can claim a right over that of his grantor. It must also appear that the grantee has no other way." For an easement by necessity claimed over the Servient Property at 125 Main St, Sacramento, CA 95814 for the benefit of Claimant's Property at 123 Main St, Sacramento, CA 95814, both elements must be shown: that Riley Chen owned both properties as a single parcel until the severance on January 1, 2015 that created them as separate parcels, and that Claimant's Property was, at that time, and remains, landlocked in the strict sense this case law describes — not merely less convenient to reach than Claimant might prefer.

HOW A PRESCRIPTIVE EASEMENT OR EASEMENT BY NECESSITY CAN BE EXTINGUISHED
California's Civil Code, in the same chapter that defines what counts as an easement (addressed in this corpus's Easement Agreement document), separately states how a servitude — the Code's general term covering an easement however it was created — is extinguished. The statute lists four ways: by the vesting of the right to the servitude and the right to the servient tenement in the same person; by the destruction of the servient tenement; by the performance of any act upon either tenement, by the owner of the servitude or with the owner's assent, that is incompatible with the servitude's nature or exercise; or, where the servitude was acquired by enjoyment (as a prescriptive easement is), by disuse of it by the owner of the servitude for the period prescribed for acquiring title by enjoyment. For a prescriptive easement, that last rule means a period of disuse matching the same five-year period that created the easement can extinguish it. An act by Claimant that is incompatible with continuing to use the easement claimed over the Servient Property at 125 Main St, Sacramento, CA 95814 — the third statutory ground — can extinguish it regardless of how long any period of disuse has run. An easement by necessity has an additional, doctrine-specific termination rule tied to the necessity itself, stated in California case law: "although a strict necessity at the time of conveyance can create an easement by way of necessity, it does not preserve it for all time" — "an easement by necessity will exist only so long as the necessity exists." An easement by necessity claimed over the Servient Property at 125 Main St, Sacramento, CA 95814 for the benefit of Claimant's Property at 123 Main St, Sacramento, CA 95814 therefore ends when the necessity that created it ends — for example, if Claimant's Property later gains its own legally adequate access to a public road — regardless of whether any of § 811's four grounds has also occurred.

CERTIFICATION: I, Jordan Alex Lee, am the Claimant identified above. I have read the foregoing declaration and know its contents. The matters stated in it are true of my own knowledge, except as to matters stated on information or belief, and as to those matters I believe them to be true.

expectedJSON.body: California has no Civil Code provision that separately creates or names an "easement by necessity" the way Civil Code § 1104 creates a different implied easement out of a transferred property's own prior, obvious, and permanent use (addressed in this corpus's Easement Agreement document). The necessity doctrine is instead stated by California's courts as case law, with two elements: "An easement by way of necessity arises by operation of law when it is established that (1) there is a strict necessity for the right-of-way, as when the claimant's property is landlocked and (2) the dominant and servient tenements were under the same ownership at the time of the conveyance giving rise to the necessity." California case law also states what "strict necessity" requires, as distinct from mere convenience: "The right of way from necessity must be in fact what the term naturally imports and cannot exist except in cases of strict necessity. It will not exist when a man can get to his property over his own land. That the way over his own land is too steep or too narrow or that other and like difficulties exist, does not alter the case, and it is only when there is no way through his own land that a grantee can claim a right over that of his grantor. It must also appear that the grantee has no other way." For an easement by necessity claimed over the Servient Property at 125 Main St, Sacramento, CA 95814 for the benefit of Claimant's Property at 123 Main St, Sacramento, CA 95814, both elements must be shown: that Riley Chen owned both properties as a single parcel until the severance on January 1, 2015 that created them as separate parcels, and that Claimant's Property was, at that time, and remains, landlocked in the strict sense this case law describes — not merely less convenient to reach than Claimant might prefer.

expectedJSON.body: California's Civil Code, in the same chapter that defines what counts as an easement (addressed in this corpus's Easement Agreement document), separately states how a servitude — the Code's general term covering an easement however it was created — is extinguished. The statute lists four ways: by the vesting of the right to the servitude and the right to the servient tenement in the same person; by the destruction of the servient tenement; by the performance of any act upon either tenement, by the owner of the servitude or with the owner's assent, that is incompatible with the servitude's nature or exercise; or, where the servitude was acquired by enjoyment (as a prescriptive easement is), by disuse of it by the owner of the servitude for the period prescribed for acquiring title by enjoyment. For a prescriptive easement, that last rule means a period of disuse matching the same five-year period that created the easement can extinguish it. An act by Claimant that is incompatible with continuing to use the easement claimed over the Servient Property at 125 Main St, Sacramento, CA 95814 — the third statutory ground — can extinguish it regardless of how long any period of disuse has run. An easement by necessity has an additional, doctrine-specific termination rule tied to the necessity itself, stated in California case law: "although a strict necessity at the time of conveyance can create an easement by way of necessity, it does not preserve it for all time" — "an easement by necessity will exist only so long as the necessity exists." An easement by necessity claimed over the Servient Property at 125 Main St, Sacramento, CA 95814 for the benefit of Claimant's Property at 123 Main St, Sacramento, CA 95814 therefore ends when the necessity that created it ends — for example, if Claimant's Property later gains its own legally adequate access to a public road — regardless of whether any of § 811's four grounds has also occurred.

By the destruction of the servient tenement; 3. By the performance of any act upon either tenement, by the owner of the servitude, or with his assent, which is incompatible with its nature or exercise; or, 4. When the servitude was acquired by enjoyment, by disuse thereof by the owner of the servitude for the period prescribed for acquiring title by enjoyment.
